handback.t:
R4-B2 (h5) is done. Full write-up with VERIFY REQUEST blocks and rerun commands: C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\results\h5_board_entry.md. All numbers are on my own synthetic worlds, not real traffic. `cargo test --release --offline --lib compact` gives 20 passing tests, and the whole lib gives 268 passing.

**Changes to `src/compact.rs` (all opt-in, defaults unchanged)**
- **Row layout:** rows are now sorted by feature id (no separate slot index) and the agent mask is `ceil(n/8)` bytes. The agent limit goes from 64 to 128, and runs of up to 64 agents pay nothing for that.
- **Bounded vocabulary:** `Vocab::bounded` / `SharedVocab::bounded` / `vocab_cap`. Lowest-hit non-keyword strings are evicted in batches, keyword strings are pinned, and recycled ids carry a generation so stale rows in other brains can never match a new string.
- **Row cap:** `max_rows` evicts the rarest rows first, using decayed guard-evidence mass.
- **12-bit cells:** `Fx12` and `Q12`, really bit-packed.
- **Binary state:** `to_bytes` / `from_bytes` (exact round trip), a state-only form `state_bytes`, and `BrainPool` for cold brains.
- **Speed work:** one-pass `decide` and a rounding/division-free u16 encode/decode.

**One existing test changed:** `byte_accounting_is_exact_for_the_u16_layout` now asserts the new per-row layout. The other 10 R3 tests are unchanged and green. The u16 representation is also no longer bit-identical to R3's because of the rounding change. The f64/f32 instances still match the shipped router exactly (diff 0.0000, identical at 3 to 128 agents).

**Equivalence**
- **Protocol:** TOST at ±0.005, with a 95% CI and Holm across the 8 worlds. The worlds are the 3 sim worlds, big-32, big-32 long-tail, big-32 open-stream, big-64 and big-128.
- **Stage 1 (declared before running, pooled 31-90 + power 91-250):** even the u16/q16 baseline could not be certified at 64 and 128 agents. At 64 agents the diff was +0.0027 [-0.0002, +0.0056]; I put this down to power.
- **Stage 2 (declared after stage 1, fresh seeds 91-450, n=360):** u16/q16 is certified in all 8 worlds, so lifting the limit to 128 agents is supported. Seeds 91-250 were already used in stage 1; the untouched seeds 251-450 alone also pass.
- **Pass:** hash32 (identical to u16/q16 here) and the bounded vocabulary at every fraction down to keywords-only.
- **Fail:**
  - **u8 weights:** -0.0105 in sim-fixed, a real loss.
  - **u12 weights and 12-bit counts:** not equivalent at 32+ agents. u12/q12 is non-inferior, but 12-bit changes behaviour (u12/q12 +0.0120 at 64 agents) and saves only 9-17% of bytes. Why is untested; my guess is that rounding stalls the weight decay.
  - **Row caps:** -0.02 to -0.055 in the sim worlds, and -0.0086 at a 50% cap in big-32. They only work in the long-tail and open worlds.
  - **Random eviction instead of value-based:** far worse, e.g. -0.013 in long-tail versus -0.0012 with value-based eviction.
  - **Cell pruning:** only a 1-3% saving at settings that pass.
- **Biggest caveat:** the tail tokens in my worlds are pure noise by construction, so a keywords-only vocabulary being harmless here is an upper bound, not evidence for real traffic. The row-cap results are the control: when evicted features carry signal, it costs quality.
- **Shared bounded vocabulary, 240 brains over one vocab:** certified at 95% in the long-tail and open worlds, but only at 90% in big-32 (CI [-0.0051, +0.0055]), so it fails my 95% rule there.

**Bytes saved**
- **Layout alone (same state):** owned bytes per trained brain drop 8% for sim-fixed, 10% for big-32 and 22% for long-tail.
- **Bounded vocabulary (largest lever that passes everywhere):** brain plus private vocabulary shrinks 74-89% in the long-tail and open worlds.
- **Binary state:** 54-62% smaller than the R3 JSON and about the size of the in-memory brain (JSON was ~2.2x memory). The round trip is exact in every world.
- **Agents per GiB:** the table shows shipped f64 router, R3 private, R4 shared vocab, R4 with a 5%-hot pool; units are thousands.

| World | f64 router | R3 private | R4 shared vocab | R4 5%-hot pool |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sim-fixed | 66.8k | 189k | 477k | 719k |
| big-32 | 4.36k | 24.0k | 56.0k | 60.2k |
| long-tail | 572 | 4.28k | 17.5k | 21.7k |
| big-64 | 2.53k | 22.5k | 45.9k | 49.0k |
| big-128 | 1.38k | n/a | 39.3k | 40.7k |

- **Open world:** 414 → 3.85k agents/GiB, because the unbounded shared vocabulary dominates (~57.7 MB for 240 brains).
- **Cold pool:** reloads and decisions are bit-exact against all-hot twins, with a median reload of 5.6 µs (sim) up to about 100 µs (long-tail) and 30 µs at big-32. It only gains 1.0-1.5x over keeping the shared vocabulary hot, and every-decision churn is 8 to 90 times slower, so spill only pays for brains that sit idle.

**Latency**
- **Method:** ns per decision, minimum over 21 interleaved reps, against a verbatim copy of the old R3 compact. The box was shared at 9-80% background CPU, so only the ratios mean anything.
- **vs R3:** the declared +10% criterion is met in all 7 worlds where R3 exists. R4 comes out at 0.85-0.99 of R3's ns.
- **vs f64:** R4 is 0.47 to 0.24 of the f64 router's ns from 6 to 64 agents, and 0.18 at 128 agents (1.9 µs versus 10.6 µs).
- **Where the speed-up comes from:** the one-pass `decide` and the rounding-free encode/decode. The sorted-row layout alone was +8 to +35% slower than R3 before those fixes.
- **Other variants vs R3:** u12/q12 packed is 0.99-1.22 and the 50% row cap is up to about 2x in the 6-agent worlds.

**Recommendation (nothing made default):**
- Keep the new layout and the 128-agent limit.
- Use a bounded or shared vocabulary for open token streams.
- Use hash32 when feature names need not be persisted.
- Use binary state for save/load.
- Do not set row caps below the signal-row count, and do not use 8/12-bit cells or cell pruning.
